opus-5.5.text:
I don't think it's really an either-or, but if I had to explain why I lean toward learning, it comes down to how the world actually looks once a robot leaves the lab.

Traditional robotics has been incredibly successful in structured settings. On a factory line you know exactly where the part will be, what it weighs, and how it will behave when you grasp it. You can write down the model, design a controller, prove some stability guarantees, and it works beautifully, thousands of times a day. I have a lot of respect for that tradition. Much of what I learned early on came from it.

The problem is that most of the tasks we actually care about don't look like that. Think about folding laundry, cooking in someone's kitchen, or manipulating deformable or articulated objects. The state space is enormous, the contact dynamics are messy, and the object you see today is slightly different from the one you saw yesterday. If you try to hand-engineer a model for every one of those situations, you end up writing exceptions to your exceptions. The engineering effort scales with the complexity of the world, and the world is very complex.

Learning flips that relationship. Instead of a human specifying every rule, you specify the objective and supply data, and the system figures out the structure. Then your effort scales with data and compute, which are things we've gotten much better at scaling over the last decade. We've seen in vision and language that once you cross a certain threshold of data and model capacity, you get generalization that nobody could have hand-designed. I think robotics is starting to see the early signs of that too.

There's also a more practical reason. Much of the knowledge about how to do manipulation tasks is tacit. If you ask someone how they tie their shoelaces, they can't really give you an algorithm. But they can show you. Learning from demonstration, or from interaction, lets us capture that tacit knowledge in a way that writing equations never could.

That said, I don't think we should throw away the classical toolbox. Physics, geometry, control theory — these give you structure, safety, and sample efficiency. Some of the most interesting work right now combines the two: using learned models for perception and high-level decisions while keeping well-understood controllers at the low level, or using simulation and physical priors to make learning more data-efficient. So for me, machine learning is the main engine for handling the open-ended complexity of the real world, and traditional methods are the scaffolding that keeps it grounded and reliable.

r001.rationale: It says hand-engineering a model for each situation leads to repeated exceptions and that engineering effort scales with the world’s complexity.

r002.rationale: It contrasts humans specifying every rule with supplying an objective and data so the system can figure out the structure.

r003.rationale: It does not connect reduced engineering labor to making robots accessible to ordinary users.

r004.rationale: It makes no comparison between current robotics and early AI agents or their dependence on expert users.

fable-5.1.text:
I'll answer directly as the guest.

Honestly, it comes down to one thing: generalization. Traditional methods in robotics are beautiful when the world matches your model. You write down the dynamics, you tune a controller, you hand-design the perception pipeline, and in a lab or a factory cell, it works great. The problem is the real world refuses to stay inside your assumptions. Lighting changes, objects deform, a cable gets in the way, the floor is slightly slippery. Every one of those edge cases becomes another rule, another special case, another month of engineering.

I spent years doing it the classical way, and what I noticed is that the engineering effort doesn't shrink as you scale. It grows. You go from ten objects to a hundred objects and your system falls apart, and the fix is more humans writing more code. That's not a path to robots that can actually operate in a home or a hospital.

Machine learning flips that. Instead of me trying to anticipate every situation, I give the system data and let it figure out the structure. The remarkable thing we've seen, especially in the last few years, is that when you throw diverse data at a large model, it starts to handle situations it never explicitly saw. That's the property classical methods fundamentally can't give you, because they only know what you told them.

Now, I want to be careful here. I'm not saying throw away control theory. If you need a robot arm to be stable at a thousand hertz, you still want a well-designed low-level controller. Physics doesn't go away. What I favor is using learning at the layers where the world is messy, perception, decision-making, adapting to new tasks, and letting the classical tools handle what they're genuinely good at, which is precision and guarantees.

So it's less an ideological preference and more a bet about where the bottleneck is. The bottleneck in robotics was never "can we compute the trajectory." It was always "does the robot understand what's in front of it." And that's a learning problem.

r001.rationale: It says new edge cases require more rules and engineering, and scaling up requires more humans writing code.

r002.rationale: It contrasts engineers manually anticipating situations and writing rules with giving data to a system that learns the structure.

r003.rationale: It mentions robots operating in homes and hospitals, but does not connect reduced human labor to access for ordinary users.

r004.rationale: It does not compare current robotics with early AI agents or discuss dependence on expert users.

astra-6.text:
For me, the appeal is that robots have to operate in a world that’s hard to describe with explicit rules. Traditional methods work very well when you have a good model and a controlled environment. But when a robot encounters an unfamiliar object or a changing environment, it’s difficult to anticipate every situation by hand. Machine learning lets us learn some of that complexity from data and experience.

I don’t see it as replacing traditional robotics, though. I favor combining them: use models and control theory where they’re reliable, and use learning for things like perception and behaviors that are difficult to program explicitly. That combination gives us a better path toward robots that can handle more than a carefully scripted demonstration.

r001.rationale: The response says hand-written rules cannot anticipate every situation, but does not state that traditional methods must be substantially re-engineered for each new task.

r002.rationale: It says machine learning learns complexity from data and experience, but does not connect that to reducing engineering labor or replacing work engineers would otherwise do manually.

r003.rationale: The response does not connect reduced human labor to making robots accessible to ordinary users.

r004.rationale: It makes no comparison between current robotics and early AI agents or their dependence on expert users.

sol-6.1.text: For me, the appeal of machine learning is that a robot has to deal with situations we can’t fully anticipate. Traditional methods work very well when we have a good model and a controlled environment. But when a robot encounters an unfamiliar object or a changing environment, it’s difficult to hand-design rules for every possibility. Learning gives us a way to improve behavior through data and experience. I’d still combine it with traditional methods—the goal is to use learning where explicit modeling becomes difficult, while keeping the structure and control that make a robot reliable.
